teile.einleitung: Cooks make sure that delicious food is served every day in restaurants, hospitals, care homes and canteens. The job requires skill, speed and great care.
wichtigste: Cooks usually work in the kitchen of a restaurant, but also in hospitals, care homes and canteens.
They prepare vegetables, fry, cook, bake and arrange the plates nicely.
In Switzerland you learn the job in the three-year apprenticeship as a cook EFZ.
Cleanliness and hygiene are especially important in the kitchen.
In large kitchens a whole team works together, known as the kitchen brigade.
Cooks often work in the evening and at weekends, when the guests are eating.

abschnitte.text: A cook prepares food. In the morning, goods are delivered and checked. After that the **preparation** begins: washing and chopping vegetables, preparing meat and fish, starting sauces. When the guests order, everything has to happen quickly. Finally, the food is **arranged** on the plate so that it also looks nice.

Most cooks work in **restaurants** and hotels. But there are many other places too: in **hospitals** and old people's homes they cook meals that suit people's needs, for example low in salt or soft. In **canteens** at companies and schools, hundreds of portions are made every day. Some cooks also work on ships or for a catering service.

If you want to become a cook, you do the apprenticeship as a **cook EFZ**. It lasts three years. You work in the training company and attend vocational school alongside. There you learn, for example, which nutrients are in foods and how to store goods correctly. For young people who find learning harder, there is the two-year basic training as a **kitchen assistant EBA**.

In large kitchens each person has a fixed task. This team is called the **kitchen brigade**. It is led by the **head chef**. A saucier is in charge of sauces, a pâtissier of desserts. This system goes back to the French chef **Auguste Escoffier**. That is why many kitchen words have French names.

In the kitchen the rule is: cleanliness first. Cooks wash their hands often and wear clean clothes. Raw meat and salad are cut on separate boards so that no germs spread. Food must be properly chilled. Because there are hot cookers and sharp knives, you work with concentration and care.

gewusst: Many technical words in the kitchen come from French, for example menu, dessert or sauce.
Cooking is a job you can do almost anywhere in the world.

teile.einleitung: Gardeners sow, plant, water and prune. Some design beautiful gardens, others raise young plants in greenhouses.
wichtigste: A gardener plants and looks after flowers, trees and shrubs.
She sows seeds and raises young plants.
She waters, feeds and prunes the plants.
Many gardeners work outdoors, others in the greenhouse.
The apprenticeship as a gardener EFZ lasts three years.

abschnitte.text: Many plants begin as a small **seed**. The gardener puts the seeds into damp soil. After a few days they germinate and tiny leaves appear. Later she moves the **young plants** into bigger pots or into the flower bed. She also grows some plants from **cuttings**, which are shoots that have been cut off.

Some gardeners plan and build **gardens**. They think about where trees, flower beds and paths will fit. They lay lawns, build stone walls and plant hedges. Afterwards they come back regularly to look after everything.

Plants need **water**, **light** and **nutrients**. The gardener waters, adds fertiliser and loosens the soil. She cuts back shrubs and trees so that they grow nicely. She can tell when a plant is ill or has pests, and knows what will help.

The apprenticeship as a **gardener EFZ** lasts three years. There are different specialisms, such as **landscape gardening** or **plant production**. If you would rather do a shorter training course, you can choose the two-year apprenticeship with a vocational certificate (**EBA**). A good eye for colours and shapes helps with design.

gewusst: In greenhouses you can grow flowers and vegetables even in winter.
Gardeners also bring more green to towns and cities, for example in parks and on green roofs.

teile.einleitung: The training company is the firm where you do your apprenticeship. There you learn the job in real everyday working life, supported by a vocational trainer.
wichtigste: An apprentice learns most of their job in the training company.
A vocational trainer shows how the work is done.
Alongside this you attend vocational school on one or two days a week.
A company needs a permit from the canton to train apprentices.
Training companies come in all sizes, from a small hair salon to a large corporation.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland you usually learn a job through an **apprenticeship**. You spend most of the time in the **training company**. There you work alongside others from the start, first with simple tasks and later more and more independently. This way you not only learn specialist knowledge, but also how to deal with customers, colleagues and managers.

The training company has a **vocational trainer**. This person is responsible for the apprentices. She explains the work, gives feedback and records in the **training report** how the apprentice is developing. To take on this role you attend a course for vocational trainers. When there are problems, she is the first person to turn to.

The apprenticeship in Switzerland is called **dual vocational training**, because it combines practice and school. There are even three places of learning: the **training company**, the **vocational school** and the **inter-company courses**, where apprentices from different firms practise the basics together. For a company to be allowed to train apprentices, it needs a **training permit** from the canton.

Before you apply, a **taster apprenticeship** is worthwhile. You work in the company for a few days and see whether the job and the team suit you. Training companies come in all sizes. In a small company you know everyone, in a large one there are often several apprentices and different departments.

gewusst: In Switzerland tens of thousands of companies train apprentices, many of them small firms.
Companies that train apprentices secure well-trained specialists for the future, because many stay with the company after the apprenticeship.

teile.einleitung: Someone doing an apprenticeship is called an apprentice (Lernende or Lernender). In the past people also said Lehrling. Apprentices have special rights and duties, which are set out in the Code of Obligations, the Vocational Training Act and the Labour Act.
wichtigste: Someone doing an apprenticeship is called an apprentice (Lernende or Lernender).
Apprentices must follow instructions and work carefully (Art. 345 OR).
Up to 18, special protection for young workers applies, for example for night work.
Apprentices keep a learning record, and the company writes a training report.
At the end of the apprenticeship the company issues an apprenticeship reference.
There is no legal minimum wage for apprentices, only recommendations from the industries.
In the EBA apprenticeship there is expert individual support if needed.

abschnitte.text: Under **Art. 345 OR**, apprentices must do everything they can to reach the goal of their apprenticeship. They follow the company's **instructions** and work **carefully**. This also includes being punctual and attending vocational school regularly. In the **learning record**, apprentices note down what they have learned. The vocational trainer checks it.

The training company regularly records, usually once a semester, in the **training report** how the apprentice is developing. This is discussed together. At the end of the apprenticeship, under **Art. 346a OR**, the company issues an **apprenticeship reference**. It describes the training and, on request, can also assess performance and behaviour.

The **Labour Act** gives young people special protection up to the end of their **18th year**. **Night work** and **Sunday work** are in principle forbidden for them. There are exceptions only for certain jobs, when they are needed for the training, for example in a bakery. Dangerous work is also restricted. In addition, apprentices up to 20 get at least five weeks of holiday a year.

Apprentices receive **wages** that rise with each year of the apprenticeship. How much they are is set out in the apprenticeship contract. There is no **legal minimum wage** for apprentices, but many professional associations give **wage recommendations**. Anyone who does unpaid youth work, for example as a camp leader, can take up to one week of **youth leave** every year until the age of 30 (Art. 329e OR).

Anyone who has difficulties gets help. In two-year basic training courses with **EBA**, the Vocational Training Act in **Art. 18 BBG** provides for **expert individual support** if needed. This person helps with learning and with personal questions. In the case of conflicts at the company, apprentices can turn to the **apprenticeship supervisors** at the cantonal vocational training office.

gewusst: The word “Lehrling” is hardly used any more today; officially people speak of Lernende (apprentices).
Many apprentices do the vocational Matura alongside their apprenticeship so that they can later study at a university of applied sciences.

teile.einleitung: Digital ethics asks what is right and fair when dealing with computers, data and artificial intelligence. It is about questions such as: may a machine make decisions about people? And who is responsible if an AI makes a mistake?
wichtigste: Digital ethics deals with acting rightly and fairly in the digital world.
An AI recruitment tool from Amazon rated applications from women lower.
The MIT experiment Moral Machine collected millions of judgements about self-driving cars.
Explainable AI is meant to show how an AI decision comes about.
Dual use means that technology can be used both for good and for harm.
Shoshana Zuboff coined the term surveillance capitalism.
Automation bias means that people trust machines too much.

abschnitte.text: **Ethics** is the part of philosophy that asks what good and right action is. Digital ethics applies this question to computers, the internet, data and artificial intelligence. It deals with fairness, privacy, responsibility and transparency. Experts from computer science, philosophy, law and politics work together on it.

In 2018 it became known that an AI recruitment tool from Amazon rated applications from women lower. The AI had learned from old applications in which mainly men had been hired. Such distortions are called **bias**. That is why people call for **explainable AI**, so that humans can understand how a decision was reached.

What should a self-driving car do if an accident can no longer be avoided? In 2016 MIT started the online experiment **Moral Machine** on this question. In it, millions of people from all over the world decided whom the car should protect when in doubt. The results showed that people from different countries sometimes judge differently.

Many free services collect data about their users and earn money from it. The US researcher Shoshana Zuboff calls this **surveillance capitalism**. Her book about it appeared in English in 2018 and became known worldwide. Digital ethics asks how much data collection is acceptable and how privacy can be protected.

Many technologies are **dual use**: facial recognition can find missing children, but can also be used to watch people. Another problem is automation bias. People often trust automatic systems too much, even when they are wrong. One example is when someone follows a satnav blindly and drives into a dead end.

Not everyone has equally good access to the internet, devices and digital knowledge. This inequality is called the **digital divide**. It exists between rich and poor countries, but also between young and old in Switzerland. Digital ethics asks how everyone can take part in the digital world.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thinking about what good and right action is.
A distortion that makes an AI treat certain groups unfairly.
A technology can be used for useful as well as harmful purposes.
Too much trust in automatic systems.

gewusst: Amazon stopped using the controversial recruitment tool after the problem was discovered.
The results of the Moral Machine, with around 40 million decisions, were published in the journal Nature in 2018.

teile.einleitung: Mechanics in the garage make sure that cars and other vehicles run safely. They check, service and repair, from changing tyres to tracking down faults with the computer.
wichtigste: A mechanic checks and repairs vehicles in the garage.
The tasks include changing tyres, changing the oil and checking the brakes.
During a service the vehicle is checked over regularly.
Modern cars have a lot of electronics, so faults are often tracked down with a computer.
In Switzerland the apprenticeships are called, for example, automotive specialist EFZ or automotive mechatronics technician EFZ.
In Switzerland vehicles must regularly go for the official vehicle inspection.

abschnitte.text: In the **garage**, the mechanic looks after cars that need servicing or repairing. He **changes tyres**, for example from summer to winter tyres. He does the **oil change**, checks the brakes, lights and windscreen wipers and replaces broken parts. With a **car lift** he raises the car so that he can see underneath it properly.

Modern cars are full of **electronics**. Many functions are controlled by small computers. That is why the mechanic often connects a **diagnostic device**. It shows where a fault is. With **electric cars** there is no engine oil change, but you work on the battery and the high-voltage system instead. This needs special training, because high voltages are dangerous.

Today the job of “car mechanic” has a different name in Switzerland. The apprenticeship as an **automotive specialist EFZ** lasts three years. The apprenticeship as an **automotive mechatronics technician EFZ** lasts four years and goes deeper into electronics. The two-year basic training is called **automotive assistant EBA**. You can specialise in cars or commercial vehicles.

A well-serviced vehicle is a safe vehicle. During a **service**, the mechanic checks the car according to a fixed plan. In Switzerland vehicles must also regularly go for the canton's **vehicle inspection**, MFK for short. Many garages prepare cars for it. In this way mechanics help to make sure that fewer accidents happen on the road.

gewusst: In Switzerland many people also call a mechanic a “Garagist”, although that word really means the owner of a garage.
A car is made up of many thousands of individual parts.

teile.einleitung: The CV is an important part of every application for an apprenticeship. It shows the company at a glance who you are, which schools you have attended and what interests you.
wichtigste: A CV includes personal details, education, taster apprenticeships, languages, hobbies and references.
For an apprenticeship one page is usually enough, two at most.
The usual form is the CV in table format.
A recent, friendly portrait photo looks professional.
Personal details include your name, address, phone number, email and date of birth.
You state your language skills with the language and the level.
The information must be correct and in a clear order of time.

abschnitte.text: A CV gives an **overview** of you and the path you have taken so far. First come your **personal details**: name, address, phone number, email and date of birth, often also your nationality. Then follow your **education**, **taster apprenticeships**, languages, computer skills and hobbies. At the end come **references**, which are people who can give information about you, for example your teacher.

abschnitte.titel: Clearly set out as a table
abschnitte.text: Today the **CV in table format** is usual. The information is arranged in columns and clear sections, often with the year on the left and the school or activity on the right. A **clear order of time** is important. Often the most recent stage is at the top. For school leavers, **one page** is usually enough, two at most. An easy-to-read font and enough spacing make it pleasant to read.

In Switzerland a CV usually includes a **photo**. It should be recent and show you looking friendly and well groomed. A simple **portrait** against a calm background is best. Selfies, holiday photos or party pictures are not suitable. The photo is often the first thing the company sees of you.

**Hobbies** say something about your personality. A team sport, for example, shows that you can work in a team, a musical instrument shows persistence, and a role in a youth group or club shows responsibility. For **languages**, you state which language you know and how well, for example native language, good knowledge or basic knowledge. This helps the company to judge you better.

All the information must be **honest**. Read your CV through several times and ask someone to check it for **mistakes**. Keep it up to date when a new taster apprenticeship is added. If you send the application by email, it is best to save the CV as a PDF. Together with the covering letter and school reports, it makes up the **application file**.

gewusst: The CV comes from the Latin “Curriculum Vitae”, which means “course of life”.
Many companies only skim a CV at first, which is why a clear structure is so important.

teile.einleitung: In data analysis, data is collected, sorted and evaluated in order to gain insights from it. Companies, researchers and authorities use it to spot patterns and make decisions. Apps and websites also constantly analyse what you click on and how long you stay.
wichtigste: Data analysis means collecting and evaluating data and drawing conclusions from it.
Big data is often described with the three Vs: Volume, Velocity and Variety.
A correlation does not automatically mean that one thing causes the other.
The median is the middle value of a sorted list and is hardly affected by outliers.
In an A/B test, two versions are shown at random to different groups and compared.
Metadata reveals, for example, who phoned whom, when and for how long.
Third-party cookies from outside providers track users across many websites.

abschnitte.text: In **data analysis**, numbers and information are prepared in such a way that you can learn something from them. A weather service, for example, evaluates measurements to forecast the weather. An online shop looks at which products are often bought together. In Switzerland the Federal Statistical Office in Neuchâtel collects data about the population, the economy and the environment. Good data analysis needs mathematics, statistics and critical thinking.

**Big data** means huge amounts of data that can hardly be handled with simple methods. Big data is often described with the three Vs: Volume for the amount, Velocity for the speed and Variety for the different kinds of data. Every day an unimaginable amount of data is created worldwide by mobile phones, websites, sensors and cameras. It is stored in large **data centres**. To evaluate it, you need powerful computers and often artificial intelligence.

The **average** and the **median** are two ways of finding a typical value. With screen times of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 200 minutes, the median is 30 minutes, the value in the middle. The average here is 60 minutes, because the one high value pulls it up. Another example is the **conversion rate**: if 50 out of 2000 visitors to an online shop buy something, it is 2.5 per cent. Such figures help you to compare data quickly.

When two things increase or decrease together, this is called a **correlation**. In a town, for example, ice cream sales and the number of cases of sunburn rise at the same time. But that does not mean that ice cream causes sunburn. The real cause is a third factor, namely sunny weather. Anyone analysing data must therefore always check whether there really is a link of **cause and effect**.

Many websites carry out **A/B tests**: two versions of a page are shown at random to different groups, and you compare which works better. Cookies store information in the browser, and third-party cookies from outside providers track users across many websites. Phone calls produce **metadata**, that is, who phoned whom, when and for how long. Even such metadata reveals a lot about a person’s life. That is why data protection is so important.

To protect people, data is often **anonymised** or **pseudonymised**. With anonymisation it is no longer possible to find out whose data it is. With pseudonymisation, the name is replaced by a number, for example. But with extra knowledge, such as a list of the numbers, the data can be linked to a person again. Pseudonymised data is therefore still considered personal data.

begriffe.erklaerung: Huge amounts of data that can only be evaluated with powerful computers.
The middle value when all values are put in order of size.
Two things change together, without one necessarily causing the other.
A comparison of two versions with groups divided at random.
Data about data, for example when and how long a call lasted.

gewusst: The three Vs of big data were described by the analyst Doug Laney in 2001; later more Vs were added, such as Veracity for trustworthiness.
Even the ancient Romans carried out censuses to plan taxes and soldiers.

teile.einleitung: The trowel is the most important tool of the bricklayer. With the bricklayer's trowel you spread the mortar so that the stones of a wall hold firmly together.
wichtigste: With the trowel the bricklayer spreads mortar between the stones.
The mortar holds the stones firmly together.
Mortar is made of sand, a binder such as cement or lime, and water.
There are different trowels for different jobs.
The apprenticeship as a bricklayer EFZ lasts three years.

abschnitte.text: First the bricklayer picks up some **mortar** with the **trowel**. Then he spreads it evenly on the bottom row of stones. He sets the next stone on top and taps it into place with the handle of the trowel. He scrapes off extra mortar with the edge. Row by row, the wall grows.

**Mortar** is a mixture of **sand**, a binder such as **cement** or **lime**, and **water**. When it is fresh it is soft and easy to spread. After a while it becomes as hard as stone. This holds the stones firmly together and keeps the wall stable.

The **bricklayer's trowel** has a pointed or rounded steel blade and a wooden handle. With the **pointing trowel** you fill narrow joints. With a **smoothing trowel** you smooth plaster. In German the same word, Kelle, is also used in the kitchen for a **ladle**, which you use to serve soup.

The apprenticeship as a **bricklayer EFZ** lasts three years. Bricklayers build walls, set up formwork for concrete walls and ceilings and work on building sites for houses, bridges and roads. A love of physical work outdoors, team spirit and precise work are important.

gewusst: The Romans already built with a lime mortar, and some of their walls are still standing today.
With a spirit level the bricklayer checks whether the wall is straight.

teile.einleitung: Painters paint walls, ceilings, building fronts, windows and doors. With paint they make houses more beautiful and at the same time protect them from weather and wear.
wichtigste: A painter paints walls, ceilings, building fronts, windows and doors.
Paint makes a house look good and protects it from damp and wear.
Before painting, the surface is cleaned, repaired and covered.
Painters work with brushes, paint rollers and spray guns.
In Switzerland the apprenticeship as a painter EFZ lasts three years.
A good eye for colours is important.

abschnitte.text: Painters work on new buildings and on renovations. They paint **inside walls** and **ceilings**, but also **building fronts**, windows, doors and railings. Paint has two jobs: it makes things look good and it **protects** them. A painted building front keeps out rain better, and a varnished wooden window rots less quickly.

Before painting, a lot of **preparation** is needed. Floors and furniture are **covered** with plastic sheeting, and edges are masked with tape. The painter fills holes and cracks with **filler** and sands them smooth. Often a **primer** goes on first so that the paint sticks well. Only then do the coats of paint follow, usually two.

The tools include **brushes** in many sizes, the **paint roller** for large surfaces and the **spray gun**. Painters know different paints and varnishes and know which is right for what. They **mix shades of colour** to the customer's wishes. Some also create patterns, lettering or special surfaces. For building fronts they work on **scaffolding**.

In Switzerland the apprenticeship is called **painter EFZ** and lasts three years. If you would rather do a shorter training course, you can choose the two-year basic training as a **painting assistant EBA**. You need skill, patience and a good eye for colours. Because you often stand on ladders and scaffolding, you should have a head for heights.

gewusst: White is the most common colour for inside walls, because it makes rooms look brighter and bigger.
In the past, painters made their paints themselves, for example from ground earth, lime and oil.

teile.einleitung: If you hand in your notice or are given notice, you cannot simply leave the next day. The notice period sets how long the employment continues after notice has been given. In Switzerland the Code of Obligations (OR) contains the most important rules.
wichtigste: After the probationary period, Art. 335c OR sets a period of one month in the first year of service.
From the second to the ninth year of service the period is two months, from the tenth year of service three months.
The period always ends at the end of a month.
Notice only takes effect when it reaches the recipient.
The periods must be the same length for employers and employees.
In case of illness there are protection periods during which the employer may not give notice.
Dismissal without notice requires a serious reason.

abschnitte.text: The **OR** sets periods that apply if the contract says nothing different. During the **probationary period** you can give notice with seven days. After that, **Art. 335c OR** applies: one month in the first year of service, two months in the second to ninth year of service, and three months from the tenth year of service. The period always runs until the **end of a month**. Different arrangements are possible, but must be agreed in writing.

Someone is in their third year of service and gives notice on **15 March**. The period is two months. Two full months are over on 15 May. Because the period has to run to the end of a month, the employment only ends on **31 May**. The day of delivery is also important: notice is a **declaration that must be received**. It only takes effect when it reaches the recipient, not on the day the letter was taken to the post office.

Under **Art. 335a OR**, the notice periods for employers and employees must be **the same length**. If the contract says something different, the longer period applies to both sides. This is so that neither side is put at a disadvantage. Anyone giving notice should ideally do so **in writing**, so that they can later prove when the notice arrived.

At certain times the employer may not give notice. These **protection periods** are set out in **Art. 336c OR**. In the case of illness or accident that is not your fault, they last 30 days in the first year of service, 90 days in the second to fifth year and 180 days from the sixth year. Notice given for unfair reasons is called **abusive**. It is still valid, but the court can award compensation of at most **six months' wages**. To get this, you must lodge a written objection before the end of the notice period.

Sometimes it is no longer reasonable to keep working together. In that case **Art. 337 OR** allows **dismissal without notice** for a **serious reason**. The employment ends immediately. A serious reason exists when, in good faith, the work relationship cannot reasonably continue, for example after a theft at the company. Courts examine such cases strictly.

gewusst: After the probationary period, an apprenticeship contract cannot be terminated with ordinary notice, but can only be ended without notice for serious reasons.
During the notice period you normally have to keep working and continue to receive your wages.

teile.einleitung: Young people need special protection at work. That is why the Labour Act (ArG) and the Ordinance on the Protection of Young Workers (ArGV 5) set out from what age, for how long and what kind of work young people may do.
wichtigste: Under the Labour Act you count as a young person until the end of your 18th year.
Regular employment is in principle only allowed from the age of 15.
From 13, light work is possible, at most 9 hours a week during school term.
Young people work at most 9 hours a day.
The daily rest period is at least 12 consecutive hours.
Lessons at vocational school count as working time.

abschnitte.titel: From what age can you work?
abschnitte.text: Under the Labour Act, **young people** are those up to the end of their 18th year. **Art. 30 ArG** in principle forbids employment under the age of 15. From 13, **light work** is allowed, for example running errands. During school term this is at most 3 hours a day and **9 hours a week**. More hours are possible during the holidays.

Under **Art. 31 ArG**, young people may work at most **9 hours a day**. This may not be longer than for the other employees in the company. Compulsory lessons at **vocational school** count as working time. So school days are included in the maximum working hours.

Young people up to 16 may work until **8 pm** at the latest, older young people until **10 pm** at the latest. Night and Sunday work is only allowed with a special permit. Between two working days, young people need at least **12 hours of rest** in one go. For adults it is eleven hours.

**Dangerous work** is in principle forbidden for young people. This includes, for example, work with dangerous machines or substances. There is an exception for apprentices aged 15 and over if the **training ordinance** for the job allows it. Then accompanying safety measures must be followed.

In the past children also worked in factories, often for many hours a day. The **Federal Factory Act of 1877** banned factory work for children under 14. It also introduced the **11-hour day**. The law is seen as a milestone in the protection of workers in Switzerland.

gewusst: Special rules apply to performances in culture, art and sport, so younger children may also take part under certain conditions.
The cantonal labour inspectorates make sure the Labour Act is followed.

teile.einleitung: Clickbait means sensational headlines or pictures on the internet whose main purpose is to make you click on them. The English word means a lure for clicks. Often the headline promises much more than the article or video then delivers.
wichtigste: Clickbait means sensational headlines or pictures that are only meant to tempt you to click.
The English word means something like “a lure for clicks” (Klickköder in German).
Clickbait works with curiosity, exaggeration and strong feelings.
Behind clickbait there is often the aim of making money with advertising.
Typical are sentences such as “You won’t believe what happened next”.
Clickbait can also lead to false news or dangerous websites.

abschnitte.text: **Clickbait** is made up of the English words “click” and “bait”. Like a worm on a fishing hook, a headline or preview picture is meant to lure people in. Usually something exciting is promised but not revealed. If you are curious, you click to find out. Often the content then turns out to be disappointing or quite different from what you expected.

Clickbait takes advantage of **curiosity**; people also speak of a curiosity gap. Typical headlines are “You won’t believe what happened next” or “Number 7 will shock you”. Words such as “unbelievable” or “shocking” and lots of exclamation marks are also common. With videos, preview pictures often show exaggerated faces, red arrows and circles. Sometimes a picture is shown that does not appear in the video at all.

Many websites and video channels earn money with **advertising**. The more people click, the more advertising is seen and the more money comes in. The algorithms of social networks also reward content with lots of clicks. That is why some people deliberately use clickbait. For serious journalism this is a problem, because exaggeration can destroy trust.

Clickbait is often just annoying, but it can also be dangerous. Some links lead to **false news** or to pages with malware. Others want to steal personal data or passwords; this is called **phishing**. So-called prize draws with “You have won a mobile phone!” are part of this too. The rule here is: do not click and do not enter any data.

A good tip is to ask yourself before clicking who is behind the **source** and what it wants to achieve. Serious media usually already state the most important point in the headline. Exaggerated promises, time pressure and lots of exclamation marks are warning signs. If you are unsure, look for the news in a well-known newspaper or on SRF. And sometimes the best thing is simply to keep scrolling.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sensational headline or picture meant to tempt you to click.
Something used to lure, for example a worm on a fishing hook.
Fraud in which someone on the internet tries to steal passwords or data.
A report that deliberately spreads false information.
Where a piece of information comes from, for example a newspaper or website.

gewusst: Long before the internet, tabloid newspapers sold more copies at the kiosk with sensational headlines.
In 2016 Facebook announced that it would show clickbait posts less often in the news feed.

teile.einleitung: Your digital identity is all the features by which you are recognised on the internet: username, profile picture, email address, passwords and much more. It is like an ID card for the online world. Because it is so valuable, you have to protect it well.
wichtigste: Your digital identity includes all the features by which you are recognised online.
A secure password is long and contains different kinds of characters.
You should use a separate password for each account.
A password manager stores many passwords securely encrypted.
In identity theft, someone uses another person’s data to pretend to be that person.
In September 2025 Swiss voters accepted the law on the state e-ID.

abschnitte.text: Your **digital identity** includes usernames, profile pictures, email addresses, posts and account details. You choose some parts yourself, for example a nickname or an **avatar**, a graphic figure that represents you online. Other parts come about automatically, for example through data that apps collect. Together they form the picture that others have of you online.

A secure **password** is long and contains capital and small letters, numbers and special characters. Passphrases made of several random words, which are easy to remember, are also good. Each account needs its own password, because otherwise all your accounts are at risk if there is a data leak. A **password manager** stores all your passwords encrypted, and you only have to remember one master password.

In **identity theft**, someone uses another person’s data to pretend to be them. The criminals, for example, order goods in someone else’s name or write messages in the victim’s name. They often get the data through phishing emails or stolen passwords. Two-factor authentication makes this much harder for them.

A **fake profile** is an account with a false identity. Some fake profiles use photos of real people who know nothing about it. They are used for fraud, bullying or to gain trust dishonestly. If you discover a fake profile with your own picture, you can report it to the platform.

The **e-ID** is a state electronic identity card for your mobile phone. A first law, under which private companies would have issued the e-ID, was rejected by voters in 2021. In September 2025 they narrowly accepted a new law under which the Confederation issues the e-ID itself. The e-ID is voluntary and is meant to help people prove who they are safely online, for example with the authorities.

begriffe.erklaerung: A graphic figure that represents a person online.
A program that stores many passwords securely encrypted.
Someone uses stolen data to pretend to be another person.
An electronic identity document you can use to prove who you are online.

gewusst: Passwords such as 123456 are among the most used every year and are cracked in seconds.
A password made of four random words is often more secure than a short password with lots of special characters.

teile.einleitung: An app is a program for a mobile phone or a tablet. With apps you can play, chat, listen to music, learn or check the timetable. The word comes from the English “application”.
wichtigste: An app is a program for a mobile phone or tablet.
Apps are usually downloaded from the app store.
You open an app by tapping its icon.
The age rating shows from what age an app is suitable.
Even free apps can cost money through purchases in the app.
Before you download a new app, you ask your parents.
Updates make sure that apps stay safe.
Apps you no longer need are deleted.

abschnitte.text: An **app** is a computer program that runs on a smartphone or tablet. Each app has a particular job, for example taking photos, writing messages or showing the weather. On the screen you see each app as a small picture called an **icon**. If you tap on it, the app opens. Some apps are already installed when you buy the phone, for example the camera or the calendar.

Apps are usually downloaded from an **app store**. On iPhones it is called the App Store, on Android phones the Google Play Store. Apple opened its App Store in 2008, and Google followed shortly afterwards. Today there are millions of apps there. The stores check the apps, but even so not every app is good or safe.

Every app has an **age rating**. It shows from what age an app is suitable, for example because of violence or because of chats with strangers. Many social networks only allow you to sign up from the age of 13. Before you download a new app, you ask your parents. With parental controls, parents can set which apps are allowed.

Many apps are free but still earn money. This works, for example, through **in-app purchases**, that is, purchases inside the app, such as new game characters or coins. Other apps show advertising or collect data about their users. Some require a **subscription** that costs money every month. That is why it is important to protect purchases on your phone with a password.

Apps are regularly improved with **updates**. Updates close security gaps, so you should install them. An app often asks for **permissions**, for example for the camera or your location. You should only allow what the app really needs. It is best to delete apps you no longer use; this saves storage space and protects your data.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for “application”, a program for a mobile phone or tablet.
An online shop where you can download apps.
A purchase made inside an app, for example for game coins.
A new version of an app that fixes mistakes and makes it safer.
Allowing an app, for example, to access the camera or your location.

gewusst: In the USA, the word “app” was chosen as word of the year 2010.
The MeteoSwiss app sends severe weather warnings straight to your phone.

teile.einleitung: Cybergrooming means that adults deliberately seek contact with children and young people on the internet in order to manipulate them and harm them later, often with sexual intentions. The offenders pretend to be good friends or to be young themselves. If you know the tricks, you can protect yourself better.
wichtigste: In cybergrooming, adults deliberately build up trust with children online in order to harm them.
Offenders often pretend to be the same age and give compliments or presents.
Contact happens in chats, social networks and online games.
If someone you only know online wants to meet you, tell your parents or a trusted person and do not go alone.
Secrets that you are not allowed to tell anyone are a warning sign.
Those affected are never to blame themselves.
Help is available from Pro Juventute on the number 147 and from the police.

abschnitte.text: The English word **grooming** really means “caring for” or “preparing”. In **cybergrooming**, adults try to win the trust of children or young people over the internet. Their aim is to manipulate the children and exploit them sexually. This often happens gradually over weeks or months. Cybergrooming is not harmless fun but a serious danger.

Offenders often pretend to be **the same age** and use fake profile pictures. They give lots of compliments, listen and act as if they understand you especially well. Sometimes they give game currency, credit or extras for games. Later they ask for photos, private information or a meeting. They often ask you to keep everything secret and to move to a private chat.

Cybergrooming can happen anywhere you can write to strangers online. This includes social networks, messenger apps and **chats in online games**. Especially when gaming, a feeling of team spirit and friendship quickly develops. That is why it is important to stay careful with strangers. Setting your profile to “private” helps you to be contacted less by strangers.

You should be careful if someone asks for photos, your address or your school. If someone says that something should stay “our **secret**”, that is also a clear warning sign. A strange feeling in your stomach is an important signal and should be taken seriously. If someone you only know online wants to meet you, tell your parents or a **trusted person**. Never go to such a meeting alone.

Anyone affected is **never to blame themselves**, even if they have already sent pictures. Help is available from parents, teachers or from Pro Juventute on the telephone number 147, also by chat. You should save chat histories with screenshots and not delete them. The police take such cases very seriously, because they may be criminal offences. Afterwards you should block the contact and report it to the platform.

begriffe.erklaerung: When adults build up trust with children online in order to harm them.
An adult you trust, for example a parent or a teacher.
A picture of the screen that you can use to show what was in the chat.
A feature that stops a person from writing to you any more.

gewusst: Offenders often deliberately use online games, because children are relaxed there and like playing with others.
On the number 147 you can get help around the clock, free of charge and confidentially.

teile.einleitung: Chimney sweeps clean chimneys and heating systems. They make sure that fireplaces and boilers work safely and that no fires break out. Their black clothing is famous all over the world.
wichtigste: Chimney sweeps traditionally wear black clothing.
Soot from the chimney shows up less on black.
They clean chimneys, stoves and heating systems.
They check whether heating systems are safe.
The apprenticeship as a chimney sweep EFZ lasts three years.

abschnitte.text: Chimney sweeps traditionally wear **black clothing**. Cleaning chimneys produces a lot of **soot**. This black dust shows up less on black. The traditional formal outfit also includes a tall black hat, the **top hat**.

When wood, oil or gas burns, soot is produced. It builds up in the **chimney**. Too much soot can catch fire and cause a **chimney fire**. That is why chimney sweeps clean chimneys, stoves and boilers regularly. For this they use brushes, balls on ropes and vacuum cleaners.

Chimney sweeps also **check** whether heating systems are working properly. They measure the exhaust gases and test whether the system is giving off too many pollutants. In this way they protect the people in the house and the **environment**. In Switzerland the **cantons** decide how often heating systems must be cleaned and checked.

The apprenticeship as a **chimney sweep EFZ** lasts three years. You should have a head for heights, because some of the work takes place on the roof. Carefulness and enjoying contact with customers are also important. After the apprenticeship, further training up to master chimney sweep is possible.

gewusst: Chimney sweeps are seen as bringers of good luck. Many people are pleased when they meet one.
At New Year you often see the chimney sweep as a lucky symbol on cards and chocolate.

teile.einleitung: A digital business model describes how a company earns money on the internet. Many apps and platforms are free, but they too have to make an income. If you know the models, you understand better why apps work the way they do.
wichtigste: A business model describes how a company earns money.
In the freemium model, basic functions are free and extra functions cost money.
On ad-funded free platforms, you pay with your attention and your data.
In real-time bidding, advertising spaces are auctioned in milliseconds.
Subscriptions bring regular income; the churn rate shows how many customers cancel.
In affiliate marketing, you earn a commission through recommendation links.
The theory of the long tail says that niche products are also worthwhile online.

abschnitte.text: Many platforms such as search engines and social networks are free for users. They earn their money with **advertising**, which is why you pay there with your attention and your data. The more a platform knows about its users, the more precisely it can target advertising. An important price is the **cost per thousand** (CPM): at 5 francs per 1000 views, 2 million views cost 10,000 francs.

In **real-time bidding**, an advertising space is auctioned while a website is loading. Various advertisers bid on it automatically, depending on who is visiting the page at that moment. The whole thing takes only a fraction of a second. The winner may show its advert to exactly this person.

In the **freemium** model, basic functions are free, and you pay for extra functions or for no advertising. Many games earn their money with in-app purchases, for example for game characters or virtual coins. Streaming services for music and films rely on monthly **subscriptions**. The churn rate is important for them: if a service with 10,000 subscribers loses 500 in a month, it is 5 per cent.

Marketplaces and booking websites often earn a fee for every sale or booking. In **affiliate marketing**, someone receives a commission when something is bought through their recommendation link. Many influencers and comparison websites use this model. For buyers this is not always obvious at first glance.

In 2004 the journalist Chris Anderson made the theory of the **long tail** well known. It says that online it is also worthwhile to sell many niche products in small quantities, because there is no shop shelf limiting space. Another principle is the **network effect**: a platform becomes more valuable the more people use it. That is why some platforms become very large and hard to push aside.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of free and premium: the basic version is free, extras cost money.
The price for 1000 views of an advert.
The share of customers who cancel within a certain time.
Advertising through recommendation links in return for a commission.

gewusst: A well-known saying goes: if you are not paying for a product, you are the product.
In German, long tail is called “langer Schwanz”; it describes the shape of a sales curve.

teile.einleitung: An apprenticeship trade is a job that you learn in Switzerland through basic vocational training. There are about 250 apprenticeship trades, from commercial employee to electrician to mediamatics specialist.
wichtigste: In Switzerland there are about 250 apprenticeship trades.
An apprenticeship with EFZ lasts three or four years, one with EBA two years.
The commercial apprenticeship is by far the most common; in 2020 more than 12,000 young people began a KV apprenticeship.
Healthcare assistant (FaGe) and retail specialist are also among the most popular apprenticeships.
FaBe stands for childcare and social care worker (Fachfrau or Fachmann Betreuung).
After an EBA apprenticeship you can often go on to a shortened EFZ apprenticeship.

abschnitte.text: Apprenticeship trades end with one of two qualifications. You gain the **EFZ**, the Federal VET Diploma, after three or four years. You gain the **EBA**, the Federal VET Certificate, after two years. The EBA apprenticeship is somewhat more practical and suits young people who find school harder. Afterwards you can often add a **shortened** EFZ apprenticeship.

The **commercial apprenticeship**, KV for short, has been the most common apprenticeship in Switzerland for years. According to the Federal Statistical Office, more than 12,000 young people began an apprenticeship as a **commercial employee EFZ** in 2020. Next come **healthcare assistant** (FaGe), with almost 5000 new apprentices in 2020, and **retail specialists**, who advise customers and manage goods.

Many apprenticeship trades are about people. **FaGe** care for and look after patients in hospitals and care homes. **FaBe**, social care workers, work for example in Kitas, old people's homes or with people with disabilities. The two-year basic training as a **health and social care assistant EBA** (AGS) supports people in their everyday lives.

**Electricians** lay cables and fit switches, sockets and systems. Their apprenticeship lasts four years. The apprenticeship as a **mediamatics specialist EFZ** also lasts four years. It combines computing, multimedia and marketing: mediamatics specialists design websites and videos and look after computers.

If you like being outdoors, you will also find many apprenticeship trades, for example farmer, gardener or forestry worker. In farming there is the two-year basic training as an **agricultural assistant EBA**. They help out on farms and in vegetable or fruit businesses. On the website **berufsberatung.ch** you can look at all the apprenticeship trades in Switzerland.

gewusst: About two thirds of young people in Switzerland do an apprenticeship after compulsory school.
With the vocational Matura you can study at a university of applied sciences after your apprenticeship.

teile.einleitung: Caretakers, in Switzerland often called Abwart, look after buildings such as schools or blocks of flats. They make sure that everything is clean, safe and in order.
wichtigste: The caretaker looks after a building and its surroundings.
In Switzerland people often say Abwart.
He cleans, repairs small things and checks the technical systems.
In a school he is an important contact person.
The matching apprenticeship is called building maintenance specialist EFZ.

abschnitte.text: In the school, the **caretaker** makes sure that everything is clean and in one piece. He unlocks in the morning and locks up in the evening. He replaces broken lamps, repairs doors and sets out tables and chairs. When there are problems he is an important **contact person** for teachers and children.

A building has a lot of **technology**: heating, ventilation, water and electricity. The caretaker checks these systems regularly. He repairs small faults himself. For bigger problems he calls in specialists such as electricians or plumbers and keeps an eye on their work.

The **surroundings** are part of the job too. The caretaker mows the lawn, trims hedges and sweeps up the leaves. In winter he clears **snow** and spreads grit so that nobody slips. He makes sure that the rubbish is sorted and disposed of properly.

The apprenticeship as a **building maintenance specialist EFZ** lasts three years. You learn to clean, repair, look after things and use machines. Later you can do further training as a **caretaker with a federal certificate**. Practical skills and friendliness are important.

gewusst: In large housing estates there is often a whole team of caretakers.
The word Abwart is used mainly in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A cook prepares the food for the guests in the restaurant kitchen. She chops, fries and cooks, and at the end the waiting staff bring the finished plates to the tables.
wichtigste: The cook prepares the food in the restaurant.
She works with knives, pans, pots, the oven and many other appliances.
Part of the work happens before the rush: the preparation, also called mise en place.
When the orders come in, everything has to happen quickly and accurately.
The kitchen and the waiting staff work closely together.
Women and men work in the kitchen equally.

abschnitte.text: The working day begins with the **mise en place**, the preparation. The cook chops onions, prepares vegetables, makes stock and gets everything ready. When the restaurant opens, the **orders** come in. Now there is frying, cooking and arranging. After service the kitchen is cleaned thoroughly, and the cook plans the next day with the team.

A restaurant has two areas: the **kitchen** and the **service**. The waiting staff take the guests' orders and pass them on to the kitchen. When a dish is ready, the cook puts the plate on the **pass**. From there the waiting staff bring the food to the guest. For this to work, both teams have to talk to each other well.

A cook also thinks about many other things. She checks whether the delivered goods are fresh. She pays attention to **allergies**, because some guests cannot eat nuts or gluten, for example. She helps to plan the **menu** and works out how much she needs to buy. This way as little food as possible is thrown away.

Restaurants are open when other people are free. That is why cooks often work in the **evening**, at **weekends** and on public holidays. In return, many have time off during the week. There are also jobs with regular hours, for example in canteens. In Switzerland the apprenticeship is called **cook EFZ** and lasts three years.

gewusst: “Mise en place” is French and means roughly “putting everything in its place”.
The Frenchman Auguste Escoffier is seen as one of the most famous cooks in history and wrote a large cookbook with thousands of recipes.

teile.einleitung: A trade union is an association of employees. Together they work for good wages, fair working hours and safe jobs.
wichtigste: Measured by number of members, Unia is the largest trade union in Switzerland.
The Swiss Trade Union Federation was founded in 1880 and is the largest umbrella organisation.
A second umbrella organisation is called Travail.Suisse.
Article 28 of the Federal Constitution protects freedom of association.
The General Strike of 1918 was the largest strike in Swiss history.
The International Labour Organization ILO has its headquarters in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: A single person carries little weight compared with a large company. Many people together can achieve more. That is why employees join together in **trade unions**. These negotiate **collective labour agreements** with the employers, advise their members and help with disputes at work.

**Unia** was created in 2004 from the merger of several trade unions, including GBI and SMUV. It mainly represents workers in industry, construction, trades and services. The **VPOD**, the union of public service staff, represents employees in administration, schools and hospitals. Many trade unions belong to the **Swiss Trade Union Federation** (SGB), others to **Travail.Suisse**.

**Art. 28 BV** guarantees **freedom of association**, which is the right to join together in associations. Strikes and lockouts are allowed if they concern working relationships. However, they must not go against a duty to keep industrial peace, as many collective labour agreements contain.

From 12 to 14 November 1918, about 250,000 people stopped work in the **General Strike**. It was led by the **Olten Action Committee**. Among other things, it demanded the **48-hour week**, the AVS and votes for women. The 48-hour week was largely introduced in 1919/1920, the AVS only in 1948 and votes for women in 1971.

The **International Labour Organization** (ILO) was founded in 1919 and has its headquarters in **Geneva**. Today it is part of the United Nations. Its structure is special: governments, employers and workers all have a say together. The ILO works for fair working conditions around the world.

gewusst: The abbreviation SGB stands for the Swiss Trade Union Federation, the oldest umbrella organisation of employees in Switzerland.
The 1918 demand for votes for women was only met at federal level more than 50 years later.

teile.einleitung: Screen time is the time you spend in front of a mobile phone, tablet, computer or television. Screens are useful and fun, but too much of them is not good for your eyes, head and body. That is why good rules and enough breaks are important.
wichtigste: Screen time is the time spent in front of a mobile phone, tablet, computer or television.
Breaks from the screen are good for your eyes, head and body.
After a long time at a screen, exercise outdoors is ideal.
Phones and tablets are not a good idea just before going to sleep.
For children, parents help to decide on screen time.
An alarm or timer helps you to stop in time.
At the family dinner table, you put your phone away.

abschnitte.text: **Screen time** includes everything you do at a screen: watching videos, gaming, chatting or watching television. Homework on the computer really counts too. Many phones count screen time automatically and show it in the settings. The Swiss **JAMES study** regularly looks at how young people use media. It shows that almost all young people in Switzerland have their own mobile phone.

If you look at a screen for a very long time, your **eyes** are often tired and dry, because you blink less while doing so. Experts recommend the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something about 6 metres away for 20 seconds. Sitting for a long time can lead to tension in the neck and back. In children who spend a lot of time indoors and look closely at screens, the risk of **short-sightedness** also rises. Daylight outdoors protects the eyes.

Phones and tablets are not a good idea just before going to sleep. Exciting videos or games keep your head awake. The bright light of screens can also make it harder to fall asleep. That is why it is good to charge your phone outside the **bedroom** at night. A book or a story before sleep helps you to switch off.

For children, the **parents** decide how much screen time is allowed. A well-known guide is the **3-6-9-12 rule** of the French psychiatrist Serge Tisseron. It recommends no screen before the age of 3 and no games console of your own before 6. You should only go on the internet alone from 9 and on social networks only from 12. Another good family rule is to put your phone away at mealtimes.

A **timer** or alarm helps you to stop in time. Many phones have a feature that suggests a break after a certain time. After gaming, exercise outdoors is good, for example cycling or playing football. Board games, crafts, reading or making music are also great things to do without a screen. During breaks, body and mind recover.

begriffe.erklaerung: Time spent in front of a mobile phone, tablet, computer or television.
An eye problem in which things in the distance look blurred.
A rule of thumb about which screen media suit which age.
A Swiss study about how young people use media.

gewusst: When you look at a screen, you blink much less often than usual, which is why your eyes become dry.
Since 2010 the JAMES study has been carried out every two years by ZHAW together with Swisscom.

teile.einleitung: Hobbies are things you like doing in your free time. They can help you choose a career, because if you enjoy doing something, you may also find a job that suits it.
wichtigste: A hobby can show what kind of work you enjoy.
If you like building with wood, you may find a career as a cabinetmaker or carpenter.
Careers advice helps you choose a career.
In a taster apprenticeship you can try out a job.
Not every hobby has to become a job.

abschnitte.text: Tim likes building things with **wood** in his free time. This shows that he enjoys working with his hands and making something you can see. Jobs such as **cabinetmaker** or **carpenter** could suit him. A cabinetmaker builds furniture, doors and kitchens. A carpenter builds roof frames and wooden houses.

If you like drawing, you may find a job in design. If you like tinkering with bikes, you might be interested in a technical job. If you like looking after animals, you can become an animal keeper. The important thing is to ask yourself: **What do I enjoy?** and **What am I good at?**

In Switzerland every canton has a **careers advice service**. There you get information about many jobs and can have conversations with advisers. Many regions have a **careers information centre** (BIZ). Parents and teachers also help in the search for the right job.

In a **taster apprenticeship** you work for a few days in a company. This way you see what the job is really like day to day. Sometimes you notice that a hobby is even more fun as a job. Sometimes you also notice that you would rather keep it as a hobby. Both are valuable experiences.

gewusst: The apprenticeships as cabinetmaker EFZ and as carpenter EFZ each last four years.
In Switzerland there are about 250 different jobs that you can learn through an apprenticeship.

teile.einleitung: At the checkout you pay for your shopping in the shop. There the goods are recorded, the prices are added up, and you pay with cash, card or mobile phone.
wichtigste: You pay at the checkout.
The goods are recorded with a scanner using the barcode.
You can pay with cash, card or mobile phone.
After paying you get a receipt.
Retail specialists also learn how to work at the checkout during their apprenticeship.

abschnitte.text: Every product has a **barcode** stuck on it. The **scanner** at the checkout reads it with light. The computer then knows immediately what the product costs. At the end the till adds all the prices together. You can see the total on the screen.

You can pay with **cash**, which means coins and notes in **francs** and centimes. If you give too much, you get **change** back. Today many people pay with a **card** or with their mobile phone. At the end you receive a **receipt**. It shows what you bought and how much you paid.

Today many shops also have **self-service checkouts**. There you scan the goods yourself and pay at the machine. Some shops have hand scanners that let you record everything while you are still shopping. Even so, staff help when something goes wrong.

If you work in a shop, you can do the apprenticeship as a **retail specialist EFZ**. It lasts three years. There is also the two-year apprenticeship as a **retail assistant EBA**. You learn to advise customers, stock shelves and work at the checkout. Friendliness and handling money accurately are important.

gewusst: Today the smallest coin in Switzerland is the 5-centime piece.
In the evening, the till is checked to see whether the money in the drawer matches the sales.

teile.einleitung: The General Data Protection Regulation, GDPR for short, is a law of the European Union that governs the protection of personal data. It has applied since 25 May 2018 and is considered one of the strictest data protection laws in the world. Swiss companies must also follow it if they have customers in the EU.
wichtigste: The GDPR has applied throughout the EU since 25 May 2018.
It protects the personal data of people in the EU.
Because of the market location principle, it also applies to companies outside the EU, for example in Switzerland.
Fines can be up to 20 million euros or 4 per cent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
Data breaches must usually be reported within 72 hours.
Users have rights such as access, erasure and data portability.
The highest fine so far, 1.2 billion euros, was imposed on the Meta group in 2023.

abschnitte.text: The **General Data Protection Regulation** was adopted in 2016 by the European Parliament and the Council of the EU. After a transition period of two years, it has applied since 25 May 2018. As a **regulation**, it applies directly in all member states, without each country having to make its own law. It replaced the older Data Protection Directive of 1995. In German it is called Datenschutz-Grundverordnung, DSGVO for short.

abschnitte.titel: Does it also apply to Switzerland?
abschnitte.text: Switzerland is not an EU member, but the GDPR still affects many Swiss companies. Under the **market location principle**, it applies to everyone who offers goods or services to people in the EU or observes their behaviour. So a Swiss online shop that delivers to Germany must follow it. At the same time, in 2023 Switzerland brought its own Data Protection Act closely into line with the GDPR. That is why the basic ideas are similar.

The GDPR gives every person important rights. With the **right of access** you can find out what data a company stores about you. The **right to erasure** allows you, under certain conditions, to have data deleted. Article 20 governs the right to **data portability**: you can receive your data in a common format and take it with you to another provider. You can also have incorrect data corrected.

Even before the GDPR, the European Court of Justice made an important ruling in 2014 in the **Google Spain** case. A Spanish man wanted old newspaper reports about his debts no longer to appear on Google. The court decided that search engines must remove links under certain circumstances. This gave rise to the so-called **right to be forgotten**. In the GDPR it is laid down in Article 17.

Companies may only process data if they have a legal reason, for example **consent**. If data is stolen or lost, the company must usually report this to the **supervisory authority** within 72 hours. Breaches can lead to fines of up to 20 million euros or 4 per cent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. In 2023 the Irish data protection authority imposed a record fine of 1.2 billion euros on Meta. The reason was the transfer of Facebook data to the USA.

The GDPR has visibly changed the internet. Since then many websites have asked for consent to **cookies**, although these banners are also based on other EU rules. Companies must explain in a privacy policy what data they collect. For many online services, children under 16 need their parents’ consent. However, individual countries may lower this limit to as low as 13.

begriffe.erklaerung: General Data Protection Regulation, the data protection law of the European Union.
The rule that the GDPR also applies to companies that offer something to people in the EU.
The right to get your data and take it with you to another provider.
The right to have certain data or search results deleted.
An office that checks whether data protection rules are being followed.

gewusst: The GDPR consists of 99 articles.
Many large tech companies have their European headquarters in Ireland, which is why the Irish data protection authority plays an especially important role.

teile.einleitung: If you like cooking at home and trying out new recipes, you can turn this into a job. The best-known job for this is cook.
wichtigste: If you like cooking, you can become a cook.
The apprenticeship as a cook EFZ lasts three years.
There is also a two-year training course as a kitchen assistant EBA.
Cooks work in restaurants, hotels, hospitals or canteens.
Other jobs also have to do with food, for example baker and confectioner.

abschnitte.text: At home, Sara likes nothing better than helping with the **cooking**. She enjoys trying out new recipes and likes it when everyone enjoys the food. The job of **cook** could suit her. In the three-year apprenticeship as a **cook EFZ** you learn to prepare dishes, present them nicely and work cleanly.

In a large kitchen a **team** works together. Each person has their own task: preparing vegetables, making sauces, frying meat or making desserts. Everything has to happen quickly when many guests eat at the same time. **Hygiene** is very important so that nobody gets ill.

Cooks often work when other people are eating: at lunchtime, in the evening and at the weekend. In return they sometimes have days off during the week. Places of work are **restaurants**, **hotels**, hospitals, care homes or canteens in companies and schools.

abschnitte.titel: Other jobs to do with food
abschnitte.text: If you prefer baking, you may find a job as a **baker and confectioner EFZ**. If you would like a shorter training course, you can become a **kitchen assistant EBA**. After the cooking apprenticeship you can train further, for example as a **diet cook**, who cooks food for people with special needs.

gewusst: At skills championships, young cooks from all over the world compete against each other.
In a professional kitchen people often call out “Service!” when a plate is ready.

teile.einleitung: The plane is a tool used to make wood smooth and straight. It takes thin shavings off the surface and is part of the basic equipment of cabinetmakers.
wichtigste: With a plane you make wood smooth and straight.
A sharp blade in the plane cuts off thin shavings.
You always plane in the direction of the wood grain.
Cabinetmakers often use the plane.
Today there are also electric planes and large planing machines.

abschnitte.text: A hand plane has a body made of wood or metal. A sharp **plane iron** sticks out a little at the bottom. When you push the plane over the board, the iron cuts off a thin **shaving**. The shaving often curls into a lovely ringlet. The less the iron sticks out, the finer the shaving.

You plane in the direction of the **wood grain**. If you plane against it, the wood tears and becomes rough. For this the board is clamped firmly onto a **workbench**. With even pressure you push the plane along the whole length. This makes the surface smooth and straight.

For large amounts of wood, joinery workshops use **planing machines**. With them, boards are quickly brought to the thickness you want. There are also **electric planes** that you guide by hand. But for fine work and repairs the hand plane remains important.

The apprenticeship as a **cabinetmaker EFZ** lasts four years. Cabinetmakers build furniture, kitchens, doors and windows. Besides the plane they need saws, drills, sandpaper and glue. Precision and a love of wood as a material are important.

gewusst: Tools similar to the plane have existed since Roman times.
The plane iron has to be sharpened regularly, otherwise the surface does not become nice and smooth.

teile.einleitung: Your digital footprint is all the traces you leave on the internet. Every post, every photo, every search and every click can be stored. These traces often stay visible for much longer than you think.
wichtigste: The digital footprint includes all the traces you leave on the internet.
There are traces you leave yourself, and traces that other people or apps collect about you.
The internet does not forget: once something is published, it can hardly be deleted completely.
Mobile phone photos can store the place where they were taken in their metadata.
Incognito mode only stops the history from being saved on your own device.
With the right to be forgotten, you can ask search engines to remove links.

abschnitte.text: Just like footprints in the snow, you also leave traces on the internet. Your **active footprint** includes everything you publish yourself, that is, posts, comments, photos and videos. Your **passive footprint** includes data that is collected without you doing much, for example websites visited, your location and searches. Websites often use small files called cookies for this.

A mobile phone photo contains not only the picture but also **metadata**. This can include the date, time, camera model and even the exact place where it was taken. If you share such a photo, you may give away where you live or go to school. Many platforms remove this data, but not all, and you can switch off location in the camera app.

A browser’s **incognito mode** does not save the history on your own device. But websites, your school, your employer or your internet provider can still see what you look at. So incognito only protects you from other people who use the same device. Apps that constantly record where you are also collect traces, so you should switch off location access where it is not needed.

Future training companies or employers sometimes search the internet for applicants. Public posts can be found through search engines, even after many years. An embarrassing photo or a nasty comment can therefore cause harm later. On the other hand, a good footprint with hobbies or projects can make a positive impression.

In app settings you can decide who sees your posts. It helps to think before posting whether you will still like the content in five years’ time. In Europe there is the **right to be forgotten**, with which you can ask search engines to remove certain links about you. Now and then it is worth typing your own name into a search engine and seeing what appears.

begriffe.erklaerung: Extra information in a file, for example the date or place a photo was taken.
A small file that websites use to recognise visitors.
A browser mode that does not save the history on the device.
The right to ask search engines to remove links.

gewusst: The right to be forgotten goes back to a ruling by the European Court of Justice in 2014.
Even people who post nothing themselves have a digital footprint, because others can share photos or names of them.

teile.einleitung: Disinformation means false or misleading information that is spread deliberately in order to deceive people. There are often political or financial aims behind it. If you know the tricks, you are less likely to fall for it.
wichtigste: Disinformation is spread deliberately in order to deceive.
Misinformation, on the other hand, is false but is passed on without bad intentions.
Social bots are automatic accounts that behave like people.
The Internet Research Agency in St Petersburg became known as a Russian troll factory.
According to an MIT study from 2018, false reports spread faster on Twitter than true ones.
Lateral reading and prebunking help against disinformation.

abschnitte.text: **Disinformation** is a deliberate lie that looks like real information. By contrast, **misinformation** is a mistake: someone shares something false but believes it themselves. Disinformation can be completely made up or can take real facts out of context. It is often meant to trigger fear or anger, because such feelings make people share things.

Behind disinformation there are sometimes states that want to influence other countries. One well-known example is the **Internet Research Agency** in St Petersburg, a Russian troll factory in which employees stirred up feeling using fake accounts. Others spread lies to earn money from clicks and advertising. Automatic **social bots** also help to repeat false messages thousands of times.

Researchers at MIT studied millions of tweets and published their study in the journal Science in 2018. They found that false reports spread faster and further than true ones. One reason is that false stories often seem newer and more surprising. In addition, it was mainly people, not just bots, who spread the false reports further.

Our brain makes things easy for disinformation. With the **illusory truth effect**, a statement seems more believable if you have heard it often, even if it is false. With **confirmation bias**, we mainly believe information that matches our opinion. If you know about these effects, you can check things more consciously.

With **lateral reading**, you open other sources to find out who is behind an unknown website. Fact-checking sites and serious media help to check claims. With **prebunking**, you learn about typical tricks of deception in advance, similar to the way a vaccination prepares the body. And before you share something, it is worth pausing briefly to think.

begriffe.erklaerung: False information spread on purpose.
False information passed on without bad intentions.
An organisation in which people deliberately stir up feeling using fake accounts.
Learning about tricks of deception in advance, to protect yourself.

gewusst: According to the MIT study of 2018, false reports on Twitter were passed on much more often than true ones.
Disinformation is not new: even in ancient times, rulers deliberately spread rumours about their opponents.

teile.einleitung: The watering can is a simple but important tool in the garden. With it, plants get exactly as much water as they need.
wichtigste: You use a watering can to water plants in the garden, on the balcony and indoors.
It has a container, a handle and a long spout.
A rose can sit at the front of the spout to spread the water finely.
Without water, plants wilt.
Besides the watering can, gardeners often also need a hose.

abschnitte.text: A watering can consists of a **container** for the water, a **handle** and a long pipe. The pipe is called the **spout**. At the front you can fit a **rose**. It has lots of small holes so that the water comes out like fine rain. This way delicate little plants are not washed away.

Plants take up water from the soil with their **roots**. Nutrients also get into the plant with the water. Without water the leaves go limp and the plant **wilts**. But too much water is also harmful, because the roots can then rot.

It is best to water in the **morning** or the **evening**, when it is cooler. Then less water evaporates. You water directly onto the soil and not over the leaves. Collected **rainwater** is particularly good for many plants.

For **gardeners**, watering is part of everyday life. Nurseries and greenhouses often have automatic watering systems. But for single pots and young plants the watering can is still practical. Florists also use it in the flower shop.

gewusst: Many watering cans hold about ten litres of water. So when they are full they are quite heavy.
Rainwater contains less lime than tap water, which some plants particularly like.

teile.einleitung: An apprenticeship place is a training position in a company where you can do an apprenticeship. The search for one usually begins in the second-to-last year of school and takes time, planning and persistence.
wichtigste: You find vacant apprenticeship places mainly on online apprenticeship exchanges such as LENA, on company websites and through contacts.
You send a speculative application to a company that has not advertised a place.
Relatives and acquaintances often know of free apprenticeship places.
An application list helps you keep track.
If you get no answer, you may politely ask after about two weeks.
For those under 18, the parents also sign the apprenticeship contract.
After an acceptance you politely withdraw from the other companies.

abschnitte.text: Many vacant apprenticeship places are listed on **apprenticeship exchanges** on the internet. A well-known one is **LENA**, the cantons' list of apprenticeship places, which you can find via berufsberatung.ch. Apprenticeship places are also advertised on **company websites**.
