abschnitte.text: The best-known task is **tying bouquets**. To do this, the florist lays the stems across each other at an angle and turns the bouquet as she goes. This creates a beautiful round shape. At the end she ties the bouquet together and cuts the stems straight.

Florists also create **arrangements**, **wreaths** and table decorations. They decorate churches, halls and tables for weddings, birthdays and company parties. For funerals they make wreaths and grave decorations. They pay attention to colours, shapes and what the customers want.

A florist knows many **flowers and plants** and knows which bloom when. She puts the flowers in fresh water, cuts the stems and removes wilted leaves. Many flowers need to be kept cool, so shops often have a cold room.

In Switzerland the apprenticeship as a **florist EFZ** lasts three years. There is also a two-year training course with a vocational certificate (**EBA**). Important qualities are a love of plants, a sense for colours, skilful hands and enjoying contact with people.

gewusst: Many florists start very early in the morning to buy fresh flowers at the market.
Before Mother's Day and Valentine's Day, flower shops are especially busy.

teile.einleitung: The driver's cab is where the train driver works. It is right at the front of the train, so that the driver can see the tracks and the signals well.
wichtigste: The driver's cab is right at the front of the locomotive or the driving trailer.
From there the train driver controls the whole train.
She watches the tracks and signals.
Many trains have a driver's cab at both ends.
Safety systems help to prevent accidents.

abschnitte.text: The **driver's cab** is at the front of the train. Through the large windscreen the train driver can see the **tracks** and the **signals**. Many trains have a driver's cab at both ends. At the final station the driver simply changes ends and drives back in the other direction.

In the driver's cab there is a lever for **accelerating** and **braking**. Screens show the speed, the power and any faults. There are buttons for the doors, lights and windscreen wipers. The train driver talks to the operations centre by radio.

To make sure nothing happens, there are **safety systems**. The **driver vigilance device** regularly checks whether the driver is awake and reacting. If she does not react, the train brakes by itself. A **train protection system** also brakes the train if it would pass a red signal or is going too fast.

Train drivers bring many people and goods safely to their destination every day. They are trained by the railway companies. Many have already completed an apprenticeship in another job before. Concentration, responsibility and punctuality are important, including on shifts early in the morning or late at night.

gewusst: On express trains on new high-speed lines, the signals are shown directly on the screen in the driver's cab.
Switzerland has one of the densest railway networks in the world.

teile.einleitung: The captain is responsible for a ship. In Switzerland captains mainly steer passenger boats on the large lakes and ships on the Rhine.
wichtigste: The captain steers the ship and is responsible for it.
Many passenger boats run on the Swiss lakes.
Some of them are historic paddle steamers.
The captain is responsible for the safety of the passengers and the crew.
Cargo ships travel on the Rhine as far as Basel.

abschnitte.text: Many Swiss lakes have **passenger boats**, for example on Lake Lucerne, Lake Geneva, Lake Zurich or Lake Thun. They take commuters and day-trippers from place to place. At the front, in the **wheelhouse**, the captain steers the boat.

The captain is the boss on the ship. He **steers** safely past obstacles and docks gently at the landing stage. He keeps an eye on the **weather** and wind, because a storm can blow up quickly on lakes. He leads the **crew**, who help with docking, check tickets and look after the passengers.

The historic **paddle steamers** are especially well known. They are driven by large paddle wheels at the side. Several of these old ships still sail on Lake Lucerne and Lake Geneva. Many passengers like to look into the engine room, where the steam engine is working.

Via the **Rhine**, cargo ships travel from the North Sea to the **Rhine ports** in Basel. This is how goods such as oil, grain or containers reach Switzerland. Anyone who wants to command a ship needs long training and a special **licence**. On the lakes, many start as deckhands and later become captains.

gewusst: Although Switzerland has no sea, there are ocean-going ships that sail under the Swiss flag.
The port in Basel is Switzerland's only access to the sea by ship.

teile.einleitung: The Gymnasium is a secondary school that prepares students for university. It ends with the gymnasial Matura, Matura for short, which opens the way to universities and the ETH.
wichtigste: The Gymnasium ends with the gymnasial Matura.
With the Matura you can in principle go to universities and the ETH without an entrance exam.
The course lasts at least four years.
Every student writes a Matura project.
With the main subject you choose your own focus.
The Confederation and the cantons recognise the Maturas together.

abschnitte.text: In some cantons you start the **long Gymnasium** straight after the 6th year of primary school. You only move to the **short Gymnasium** from secondary school. According to the recognition regulations, the path to the Matura lasts at least **four years**. In some cases a year of secondary school counts towards this.

At the Gymnasium you learn languages, maths, natural sciences, history, art and more. With the **main subject** you choose your own direction. Examples are Latin, biology and chemistry, or economics and law. There is often also a **supplementary subject**.

Every student writes a **Matura project**. This is a larger piece of independent work on a topic you choose yourself. You research, write, build or design something and present the result at the end. This way you learn how scientific work is done.

With the gymnasial Matura you can in principle go to **universities** and the **ETH** without an entrance exam. For medicine there is sometimes an aptitude test. For many courses at a **university of applied sciences** you also need about a year of experience in the world of work, for example an internship.

For a Matura to count throughout Switzerland, it has to be recognised. This is arranged jointly by the **Confederation** and the Swiss Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education (**EDK**). The Gymnasiums themselves are run by the cantons.

gewusst: Besides the gymnasial Matura, Switzerland also has the vocational Matura and the specialised Matura.
If you do not do the Matura at a Gymnasium, you can also do it later, for example at a Matura school for adults.

teile.einleitung: Career planning means thinking about your own path at work: what interests me, what can I do, where do I want to go? Because the world of work and people change, you do not plan your career just once, but again and again.
wichtigste: John Holland divides career interests into six types, the RIASEC model.
Edgar Schein described career anchors, which are values that people hold on to during their career.
Donald Super showed life roles as the “Life-Career Rainbow”.
With “Planned Happenstance”, John Krumboltz showed that chance events can also be opportunities.
SMART goals help you to express career goals clearly and in a way that can be checked.
Besides the management career path there is the specialist career path for experts.
In Switzerland, viamia offers a free career assessment from the age of 40.

abschnitte.text: The American psychologist **John Holland** sorted career interests into six types: realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising and conventional. From the English initial letters it is called the **RIASEC model**. The “E” stands for “enterprising”: such people like to lead, persuade and sell. Most people fit two or three types, and jobs can be sorted in the same way.

**Edgar Schein** found that people hold on to certain values during their career, for example security, independence or leadership. He called them **career anchors**. **Donald Super** saw a career as a lifelong development. In his **“Life-Career Rainbow”** he shows roles such as learner, worker, citizen or family member, which overlap across the stages of life.

Not everything can be planned. With his approach of **“Planned Happenstance”**, **John Krumboltz** stressed that unplanned events are often important opportunities: a conversation, a holiday job, a new hobby. Curiosity, persistence, flexibility and optimism help you to recognise such chances. So good career planning combines clear goals with openness.

Goals become concrete when they are **SMART**: specific, measurable, attractive, realistic and time-bound. Instead of “I want to improve”, a SMART goal would be something like “I will complete a spreadsheet course by the end of the year”. There are two ways to move up: on the **management career path** you lead a team, on the **specialist career path** you deepen your knowledge as a specialist or expert.

Every canton has a **careers, study and career guidance service**. There, specialists help with choosing a career and with later questions, for example a change of job. With **viamia**, the Confederation and the cantons have created a service that has existed throughout Switzerland since 2022. People aged 40 and over can use it to have their work situation reviewed free of charge and receive recommendations.

gewusst: Many interest tests used in careers advice are based on John Holland's RIASEC model.
Edgar Schein described eight different career anchors.

teile.einleitung: Wages are the money you get for your work. Apprentices also work in the company and receive apprentice wages for it every month.
wichtigste: In Switzerland apprentices receive apprentice wages every month.
Apprentice wages rise a little with each year of the apprenticeship.
The gross wage is the wage before deductions; the net wage is what is paid out.
Contributions to social insurance such as the AVS are deducted from wages.
Switzerland has no national minimum wage, but some cantons have introduced one.
How high wages are depends on the job, experience and the industry.

abschnitte.text: If you do an apprenticeship, you work in the company and receive **apprentice wages** for it. They are lower than the wages of trained specialists, because you are still learning. The wages rise a little with each **year of the apprenticeship**. How much they are is written in the apprenticeship contract. Many professional associations give **recommendations** on this.

There are two important figures on the payslip. The **gross wage** is the agreed wage. Contributions are deducted from it, for example for the **AVS**, disability insurance and unemployment insurance. What is left is the **net wage**, which is transferred to your account. The deductions are not lost: they protect you, for example in old age or if you become unemployed.

Switzerland has no national **minimum wage**. A popular initiative calling for one was rejected at the ballot box in 2014. However, some **cantons** have introduced their own minimum wage, first the canton of **Neuchâtel**, and later also, for example, Geneva, Jura, Ticino and Basel-City. In many industries, **collective labour agreements** set minimum wages.

Your first wages also bring responsibility. It is worth making a **budget**: how much do I spend on my phone, clothes and free time, and how much do I save? It is often agreed that apprentices contribute part of their wages at home as **board money**. If you learn to handle money early, you avoid debt.

gewusst: The word “salary” comes from the Latin “sal”, which means salt.
From 1 January after their 17th birthday, people in work in Switzerland pay AVS contributions.
